#3389. ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Returns Lionsgate Franchise To Fortune With $120M+ U.S. Opening – Box Office Update

SATURDAY AM: Lionsgate has gotten The Hunger Games franchise back in the $100M+ opening range that this Suzanne Collins IP is known for on the big screen as the sixth film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, is now posting a $120M North American start after a $56M Friday, which includes previews. In addition, the CinemaScore jumped from a B+ on the last film, Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, to an A- here.

PostTrak exits have increased to an 80% definite recommend, and 93% positive. The pic is playing evenly throughout the nation, however, strong in South, South Central, Midwest and Mountain. PLFs and Imax are repping 47% of the weekend (15% Imax, 32% PLFs). AMC Lincoln Square is the highest grossing venue for the Francis Lawrence directed title at $168K as of Friday.

Walk-up business for Sunrise on the Reaping was 36% yesterday in PostTrak exits (meaning those who purchased tickets same day). That’s similar walk-up business to Wicked two years (37%), and higher than last year’s Wicked: For Good (26%), but it’s lower than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (47%). Realize though that movie didn’t have a majority of fans buying tickets in advance like Sunrise on the Reaping (54% to 64%).

Women at 68% remain the big turnout for the latest Hunger Games movie which is no surprise. Forty-nine percent of the women who saw the movie came with one friend or more to watch the film (similar to Songbirds & Snakes 50% who came with one to five people), while 22% came with a date, spouse or partner (same as the 2023 film). The overall audience at 64% bought tickets because it’s for a franchise they love, while 33% said it was because of the cast.

Diversity demos on Sunrise on the Reaping are 49% Caucasian, 27% Latino and Hispanic, 9% Black and 9% Asian American, which is similar to the previous pic’s 50% Caucasian, 24% Latino and Hispanic and 10% apiece for Black and Asian American audiences. The percentage of 18-34 year olds showing up remained huge at 74% for Sunrise versus 76% for Songbirds & Snakes.

Sunrise on the Reaping currently is the fourth best opening in the franchise, but will likely be the third best, overtaking 2014’s Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 ($55.1M Friday/previews and $121.8M 3-day) by tomorrow. The top two domestic starts in the Collins series are 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9M Friday/previews, $158M 3-day) and the original 2012 Hunger Games ($67.2M Friday/previews and $152.5M opening). Catching Fire stills stands as Lionsgate’s top opening at the domestic B.O.

Amazon MGM Studio’s I Play Rocky is coming in ligher than expected with $9.3M despite scoring a rare A+ CinemaScore (which no Rocky movie in CinemaScore history has done even though this pic is about the making of the 1976 Sylvester Stallone movie). Note the movie is older skewing with 52% over 45, and that audience will take their time to come out, likely discovering the movie later this week. The exits here are powerful enough with an 87% definite recommend. 59% to 41% male-to-female with 50% men over 25, 37% women over 25 and 9% men under 25 and 5% women under 25. Very strong positive scores and definite recommends in every single demo. Caucasian turnout at 57%, Latino and Hispanic at 22%, Black at 8% (giving pic a 100%), Asian American at 7%, and Native American at 7% (also a 100% score).

No major PLFs on this pic. The Peter Farrelly directed movie is playing best in the West, East and South Central. To give you an idea of how older skewing it is, the Cinemark Palace 21 in Boca Raton, FL is the leading single-location gross at $11.2K yesterday.

The entire theatrical marketplace is around $172.1M, just -5% off from a year ago when Wicked: For Good opened to a franchise best of $147M. With no Moana, Zootopia, or Wicked in the marketplace, there was some concern that we would hit a dry spell at the Thanksgiving box office, which would be unfortunate given the great resurgence we’ve had at the domestic box office, now coursing to $9B by the end the holiday with an eye at $10B by the end of the year. Thanks to Lionsgate, Sunrise on the Reaping is going to get us through. With Disney’s Hexed and Universal’s Focker-in-Law expected to post around $45M a piece over the Wednesday-Sunday stretch, it wouldn’t be shocking if Hunger Games takes the lead with $50M+ over the 5-day box office as the franchise typically rallies over the Thanksgiving holiday.

Focus Features’ highly buzzed Andrew Scott Best Actor movie Elsinore is seeing a solid opening theater average of $40K from 6 theaters in NYC and LA for a 3-day of $240K. Friday was $140K with $33K coming from AMC Lincoln Square and LA’s AMC Grove with $32K. Both had Q&As boosting ticket sales. RT critics are at 87% certified fresh.

Top Hunger Games openings at the North American B.O. belong to 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9M Friday/previews, $158M 3-day); the original 2012 Hunger Games ($67.2M Friday/previews and $152.5M opening), and 2014’s Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 ($55.1M Friday/previews and $121.8M 3-day). Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the Collins’ franchise, the fifth directed by Francis Lawrence. Altogether the previous five movies count $3.3 billion at the worldwide box office.

Again, the jaw drop here is how this franchise turned its fortunes upward after hitting an all-time low in its opening three years ago with Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6M). Comps to other sixthquels are hard, and the opening jump between Songbirds & Sunrise is +147% — which is unheard of. The surge in domestic openings between Christopher Nolan’s Batman Begins and Dark Knight was +225%.

Among all openings in November at the domestic B.O., Sunrise on the Reaping is currently 13th in a list of 16 movies that have bowed to over $100M for the month.

RelishMix beams that the great word-of-mouth that the pic has “book loyalists showing up in full force, insisting this adaptation finally respects the source material. There’s trust running through the comments, ‘Director Francis Lawrence’s track record and the franchise’s unbroken prequel streak as reasons to believe this one sticks the landing,’ and, ‘We’ll need therapy after this,’ read as proof of the story’s emotional weight. Comments marvel, ‘Dang from Voldemort, Moriarty, Hades, and Ramses to President Snow, Ralph Fiennes catching literary villain roles like Pokémon.’ Others draw sharper comparison, saying ‘this is like the and/or of the Hunger Games I feel it, I know it, I read the book and they are going to break your heart.'”

Overall social media reach is 652M across TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, X and Facebook which is not far from The Odyssey‘s pre-opening reach at 680M and +66% above where Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes was in its social media universe, bowing shortly after the actors strike ended (393M). That 652M reach for Sunrise on the Reaping is 95% above other action-sci-fi-fantasy sub-genre features.

Sunrise‘s money is currently the second-best previews YTD after Sony’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($72M, $360M) and ahead of Universal’s The Odyssey ($17.6M previews, $123.5M opening).

RELATED: All The Best Picture Oscar Winners – Photo Gallery

Other previews that Sunrise on the Reaping is beating include Universal’s Wicked from two years ($19.2M; $112.5M opening); for the longest time we heard that the latest feature take of a Suzanne Collins novel was outstripping the presales of that female-skewing musical starring Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo. It’s also ahead of Lionsgate’s Michael ($12.6M previews, $97.2M opening), The Devil Wears Prada 2 ($10M, $76.7M opening) and light years ahead of the previous Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ($5.75M previews, $44.6M opening), which had its campaign impacted by the 2023 actors strike, not to mention the Collins novel about the origins of Coriolanus Snow wasn’t a fan fave. Sunrise on the Reaping was beloved by fans in its early story about the Woody Harrelson mentor character, Haymitch Abernathy.

When it comes to the all-time preview record for a Lionsgate title, that belongs to The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2, which made $30.4M from midnight shows leading to a $141M opening back in mid-November 2012.

Catching Fire‘s back in the day began warming up with 10 p.m. Thursday night shows. Note that Wicked‘s previews were composed of Amazon promotional screenings, Wednesday night PLF shows and an $8M Thursday.

With a great preview start, it’s fair to say that a $100M opening is well in store for the net-$150M priced Sunrise on the Reaping, especially with a 95% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is the best ever in the franchise ahead of Catching Fire (89%), Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (89%), Hunger Games (81%), Mockingjay Part 2 (71%), and Mockingjay Part 1 (66%).

Overseas, industry projects have risen from a $70M forecast to $86M opening.

Ever since the Mockingjays (both at 70%), critics’ love for Hunger Games has waned with Songbirds and Snakes being the worst reviewed in franchise at 64%.

The Hunger Games franchise through its five previous movies has minted $3.3 billion at the global box office.

#3387. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3386. ‘Percy Jackson’: How A Quest To Save Annabeth Makes Everyone Reevaluate Their Relationships In Season 3

SPOILER ALERT! This post contains some details from the first two episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3.

If there is one thing that the kids of Camp Half-Blood can count on, it’s that their lives are only going to get more complicated.

Percy Jackson and the Olympians returned to Disney+ for Season 3 on Friday, and already the dynamics have shifted. The first episode opens with Percy (Walker Scobell) and Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) recruiting the recently revived child of Zeus, Thalia (Tamara Smart), to help them rescue two younger demigods — Nico and Bianca di Angelo, the children of Hades — and the tension is palpable. Related Stories Casting 'Afterlife With Archie' Disney+ Series Casts Its Archie, Veronica, Betty, Jughead & Sabrina News 'Gilmore Girls: A Year In The Life' Gets New Home On Hulu After Netflix Deal Ends, Release Date Set

“I think that Annabeth’s presence is actually incredibly divisive between the two of them,” Smart tells Deadline of the dynamic between Thalia and Percy. Watch on Deadline

In terms of sowing that division on screen, she adds that “a lot of it is based in our actual relationship in the best of ways.”

“Walker also has the exact same personality and sense of humor. So, right right off the bat, we were definitely going back and forth and joking, and I think the only thing we had to do was just up the stakes and be serious about it, which was actually more difficult than we planned,” she says.

Percy and Thalia can’t agree on almost anything, except their loyalty to Annabeth, who has unwittingly been thrown in the middle of their power struggle at the start of the season.

So, when Annabeth is captured and brought to an enemy stronghold where she’s forced to bear the weight of the sky (the eponymous Titan’s Curse), those two have to set aside their differences quite quickly.

“She kind of kept them at a safe distance away from each other, because, as I guess we’ve seen the trailer, bad things happen when they’re not at that safe distance,” Scobell says. “So I think without her there, they’re forced to actually work together and try to figure each other out and attempt to understand each other.”

Adds Smart: “They actually have to be forced into proximity to work together to get her back, because that’s their mutual interest. So, it’s really beautiful in a way that her absence brings them closer, which is a very human thing for us. I think as people, we’re just always brought closer by tragedy. But I think that for them specifically, a lot of ego has to get out the door for them to work together to achieve their mutual goal.”

Rather than put a wedge in Annabeth’s relationship with either, Jeffries thinks that the tension between Percy and Thalia also provides some clarity for the daughter of Athena. Whether she’s ready to face that realization yet is another story.

“I honestly feel like you get to see more Percabeth when it’s between Percy and Thalia,” Jeffries says. “I feel like her eyes open up a little bit. Annabeth is very smart. Even though she’s making it look like she’s not noticing, she knows [she’s developing feelings for Percy]. I don’t know if that’s more of like a denial between her of like, ‘No, no, I’m working right now. I’m on missions. I don’t have time to be falling in love…’

She continues: “You get to see the fight [in her] more, not physically, but just like ‘No, I love this person. You’re not gonna take him away from me.'”

#3385. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3384. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

But before you buy the new-and-improved Oura Ring 5, there are some hidden costs to consider. First, you need a sizing kit.

The Oura Ring 5 holds the title of the "world's smallest smart ring", with a focus on a slim design and lightweight barely-there feel.

After wearing the Oura Ring 5 for five months, I must say that it lives up to its title. Not once have I ever felt any discomfort from wearing the ring, with its sleep design never interfering with my sleep. Thanks to the sizing kit, it fits like a glove, too.

The Oura Ring 5's fit was a breath of fresh air compared to the Apple Watch Ultra that I wore to bed for a few months before I obtained the Oura Ring 5. Granted, the Apple Watch Ultra is a lot bigger and bulkier than the newer Apple Watch models, such as the Apple Watch 12.

But all Apple Watches are exactly that: watches. I find any wristwatch uncomfortable to wear in bed, particularly smartwatches with heavy screens and tight straps (you need plenty of skin contact for tracking accuracy). But that's a personal preference and if you don't mind something bulky on your wrist in bed, you might sleep happily in the Apple Watch 12.

As for the Garmin, the lead tester in our Garmin Index Sleep Monitor review found the armband design to be surprisingly comfortable and lightweight. The band is available in two sizes (S-M and L-XL), and its screen-free design means it isn't weighed down by heavy monitors.

When it comes down to it, the Oura, Apple, and Garmin sleep trackers share a lot of core sleep tracking features. For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

You can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. When I wore the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch (Ultra) at the same time, I felt the Oura Ring's data reflected how I felt in the morning more accurately than the Apple Watch. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That said, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

Our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, said that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

It's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. And its unique circadian scoring, which uses sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype, can help you identify how well your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide around six to nine days of battery life on a single charge. A full charge (from zero to 100) is said to take up to 80 minutes, though I find it charges much faster than this.

That said, I've never found that my ring's battery life has lasted nine days (or even a full week), but this may be due to the fact that I wear a size 7 — the smaller sizes have a shorter battery life.

However, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

The Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You want in-depth sleep tracking: The Oura Ring 5's accuracy is renowned, while its unique sleep features (such as its Body Clock feature) sets it apart.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

#3381. Six new Aqara smart lights with Apple Home support and ‘spatial intelligence’

Aqara has announced the global launch of six new smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the company describes as “spatial intelligence.”

The new lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization …

All of the new products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the new products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the new products in the company’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

Pricing ranges from $24 for new light bulbs through to $320 for the 100-foot-long permanent outdoor rope lights. You can find all the new products here.

#3380. Netflix’s ‘Minimum Wage’ Ushers In Streaming’s Short Ep Sitcom Era: “The Future Is 15-Minute ‘SpongeBob’-Length Episodes”

In a world of increasingly short attention spans, social media slop and doomscrolling brainrot, it’s a wonder why many television shows got longer in the streaming era.

Case in point, the 22-minute broadcast sitcom was largely replaced by the 30-minute dramedy and the 43-minute procedural has been overshadowed by the hour-long premium drama series.

Netflix, however, has found success with a much shorter concept in Minimum Wage.

The comedy series, which comes from Jeremy Garelick and Will Phelps’ American High, consists of 14 episodes between 12 and 20 minutes in its first tranche, which debuted at the end of October.

Set in a pizza joint and starring new SNL darling Grace Reiter, Aidan Micho, Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Luke Burke, Ryan Micho, Tommy Armstrong and Randall Park, its short episodes are a feature, not a bug. Watch on Deadline

Phelps told Deadline, “The future is these 15-minute kind of SpongeBob-length episodes where it’s really fast. There’s not any fat.”

In fact, Netflix demanded short episodes for the show, which began life as a series of YouTube sketches shot during the middle of the night with interns as camera operators and a building manager handling the boom mic.

Garelick said, “When we closed the deal, [Netflix] said that they wanted it to be a minimum of twelve and a half-minute episodes. It was an interesting challenge because most episodic TV shows are 22 to 30 pages. It was almost like we were inventing a new structure as we were going and it was hard.”

Episodes were also capped at 20 minutes with shooting scripts ending up being around 15 pages and the cast encouraged to improv. “You can captivate an audience for 15 minutes really well,” Phelps added. “Jeremy and I are coming at it from traditional screenplay writing and the cast is coming at it from making the most exciting one-minute thing for TikTok or Instagram.”

This contrast is both the essence of Minimum Wage and also highlights one of the industry’s challenges as creators such as Druski and others are increasingly working on scripted projects for streamers.

“Everyone’s clamoring for creators to make shows now [following] the success of Obsession and Minimum Wage and I’m nervous that without the guidance of traditional screenwriters, you might fall into a trap of creators that are used to taking a one-minute premise and being told expand that into 15 minutes. That’s just going to be full of fat. Whereas we’re taking stories that really should be a half-hour and squeezing the fat out from the other side. That’s the secret sauce that we have.”

Garelick began his career working as an assistant for Joel Schumacher and working on movies such as The Break-Up and The Wedding Ringer before teaming up with Phelps to buy a high school in upstate New York, where they made films such as Banana Split, Holly Slept Over and Pete Davidson-starrer Big Time Adolescence.

“We’ve become a traditional Hollywood studio, but we give a lot more trust to the creators and the artists, and we have an academy, our shorts and our sketch teams, and we’re kind of combining [it all],” said Garelick.

This also allowed American High to deliver more episodes of Minimum Wage than Netflix had originally ordered. The streamer initially greenlit 20 episodes but they ended up writing 28 scripts and persuaded Netflix that it would be cheaper to produce them all.

“We don’t get hung up on the actual business side of things. We’ll just do it for the love of the game,” added Phelps.

Minimum Wage debuted last month and reached Netflix’s global top ten charts with 2.4M views, impressive given the season’s run time is under four hours.

It is one of a number of streaming shows keeping episode lengths concise. Shane Gillis’ Netflix comedy series Tires is generally in the 20-23-minute range, while HBO Max’s The Big Bang Theory spinoff Stuart Fails To Save The Universe consists of episodes between 18 and 20 minutes with one episode clocking in at only 15 minutes.

Co-creator Chuck Lorre, who has spent the vast majority of his career working in broadcast comedy, said there was “no real reason” to pad the episodes. “The historic length of a show is entirely arbitrary, it comes from network television where a certain amount of advertising has to be sold to pay the way of making this television, but it’s not an element any longer in streaming,” Lorre said. “So, why not just make the best show we can and hope the audience is entertained and is not looking at their watch.”

Minimum Wage works because it is a workplace comedy, one featuring an overwhelmed group of teenagers struggling to run The Slice Club, where the “stakes are low and the pressure is immense.”

It’s not clear whether the remaining 14 episodes that American High shot will be labeled as the second part of season one or season two, but they are expected to air in spring 2027. There’s also plenty of road for more episodes; Garelick said that they’ve already got around 50 more draft scripts.

“It takes a few months to get there, and then it takes a year or so of incubating that online to get a fan base, and then you’re ready to start a show with some solid footing behind it, and the audience feels like they were part of the inception of this,” said Phelps. “I think it’s the future of TV.”

#3378. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

#3377. Amazon’s all-in-one cheap soundbar has a built-in subwoofer for under $250 — there's just one thing holding it back

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is an admirable entry-level soundbar. Although it won’t beat any of the big names unlike its cheaper sibling, the TV Soundbar, it provides an instant TV speaker upgrade without breaking the bank.

Built-in subwoofer with adjustable bass volume

Bass can overpower dialogue in action scenes

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Price: 4/5Sound quality: 3/5Design: 4/5Features: 3/5Overall score: 3.5/5Best for: The space-conscious, budget-conscious, subwoofer-wanters

All-in-one soundbars are a dangerous game. How does one balance center channels for dialogue with a subwoofer for the best blockbuster movie action? In the case of the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, with semi-difficulty.

Don’t get me wrong, the price is incredibly appealing — $249 for a 3.1-channel soundbar is super affordable — and the minimalist design won’t cause any controversy. But is this enough to make it one of the best soundbars?

Yes and no. Unfortunately, the bass tends to overpower dialogue in action-heavy scenes. But could this still be the soundbar for you if you only watch TV and YouTube? Find out in this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus review.

If you’re looking for a reason to buy the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, that sweet, sweet MSRP is the biggest one.

At $249 at Amazon U.S. ($139 on sale) and £249 at Amazon U.K., the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is incredibly cheap for what you get. It’s an all-in-one “Dolby Atmos” soundbar — yes, that means with a built-in subwoofer. The basic model, Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, is $119, so you’re essentially paying $130 for a built-in subwoofer.

At this price point, there’s very little competition. Of course, there’s the Samsung B750F ($297, 2025 model), which has a separate subwoofer and 5.1 channels (more upfiring speakers for better surround sound). Even so, this is $50 pricier, which can be a dealbreaker if you’re on a rigid budget.

I’ve also tested the Samsung Q600F — MSRP of $499 but often on sale in the $300s — which is 2025’s model but has a 3.1.2 channel setup, which is the minimum you need for genuine Dolby Atmos. I’ll get into this more below, but that’s the long and short of it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349 with a 3.1 channel — so the same as the Amazon Plus and without the surround channels present on the Samsung Q600F — which I would recommend over the Plus if you have a little more to spare. Its separate subwoofer provides a stronger bass response without overpowering dialogue, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

Like the $119 Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus model also has EQ modes. These are as follows: “Music”, “Movie”, “Sports”, and “Night”. There’s also individual bass level adjustment if you want to get really particular with your listening experience.

There's a dialogue mode, but this didn't isolate speech as well as I wanted it to, especially in louder, action-heavy scenes.

Music mode (connected via Bluetooth) is fine, although the bass was a little boomy and the vocals a little too sharp. I would recommend grabbing one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7, to listen to music at home.

So let’s get one thing straight: the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus does not have “true” Dolby Atmos. If a soundbar doesn’t have side-firing or up-firing channel speakers, it physically cannot project soundwaves in that way.

In Top Gun: Maverick's dogfighting scene, I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV

However, the Plus has “Dolby Atmos”, which means it can technically decode Atmos signals. While this obviously doesn’t produce a genuinely immersive experience, it does have its moments. In the dogfighting scene in "Top Gun: Maverick," I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV. As I’ll get into later, this pushed the dialogue to the back of the soundstage, resulting in me straining to hear speech.

Dolby Atmos was better in “K-Pop Demon Hunters, which is really surprising. Usually, “Top Gun: Maverick” blows other movies out of the water in terms of Atmos. Cheering crowds were louder and more immersive in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," and some dialogue was positioned well in the up-firing speakers. One character's voice was particularly crisp and immersive — the lowest female voice — which makes me think the soundbar is better at isolating lower mids than sub-bass.

Despite having a range of EQ modes and a palatable price, unfortunately, the Plus gets a 3.5-star rating from me for a reason. There's one majorly important thing holding it back.

Unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus really struggles to differentiate between dialogue and bass layers in action-heavy scenes. “Top Gun: Maverick” was particularly egregious here: Bass often overpowered dialogue, especially when the soundtrack was relatively heavy in flying scenes. I could barely hear Maverick's radioed dialogue to the characters in the control room over the string-heavy soundtrack and the flying airplane.

This was incredibly surprising, as the cheaper non-Plus model excelled in the very same scene. Bass volume was set to the minimum, and I watched on “Movie” mode.

While not as egregious in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," I still struggled to hear some dialogue. Surprisingly, the music sounded excellent in this movie, but dialogue is arguably the most important part. If you can’t hear the actors, what’s the point?

The consequences are really enormous: I struggled to make out dialogue in action-heavy scenes across the three movies I watched, which isn’t really what you want when using a soundbar. The whole purpose of a soundbar is to make dialogue more intelligible.

However, I also watched "Gilmore Girls" on basic Netflix, which sounded great. If you predominantly watch TV or YouTube, I don't think you'll notice this issue. It's just a concern for action movie buffs. In that case, I'd recommend checking out the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375).

At $249, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is incredibly affordable. There are very few soundbars that can beat this in terms of penny-per-performance.

The aforementioned Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349, so $100 more than the Amazon model, but has a dedicated subwoofer and a center channel for dialogue. I would personally save up more and buy the Sony model over the Amazon.

But if I were to save more money, I'd choose the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar (non-Plus) over the Plus version. Sure, there's no subwoofer, but it's just $119 and genuinely sounds fantastic. It's the best budget soundbar I've ever tested.

Hmm. This is a tricky one. I loved the basic Amazon Fire TV Soundbar — if you want seriously great sound at a low price, get that one. The extra $130 for the Plus model? Not worth it, if you ask me. I would either spend an extra $50 on the Samsung B750F or an extra $130 on the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer.

Unfortunately, due to a lack of communication between the built-in subwoofer and the main channel speakers, dialogue can be overpowered during action-heavy scenes. Consequently, I can’t recommend this model over the Samung B750F. Personally, I would either get the cheaper Amazon Fire TV Soundbar or the aforementioned Samsung model. Or, you could save up a little extra for the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375) or the with Rears version ($489).

However, if you have an Amazon Fire TV and want something capable of integrating into the ecosystem seamlessly (even though you'll need a separate Fire stick or Fire TV), without having to spend an extra $50 on the B750F, the Plus is a great deal.

Leaker Ice Universe says Apple is currently developing four models of the 20th anniversary iPhone which we’ve been referring to as the iPhone 20. We’re expecting next year’s flagship models to be a radical new design with an all-glass appearance.

Why four models rather than two is unclear, but it seems possible Apple is testing two versions of both the Pro and the Pro Max to determine just how ambitious it can be with the final product …

Didn’t the iPhone 6 or the iPhone 11 already have a curved front glass?

Apple has been prototyping this quad-curved design for three years, making several revisions along the way—particularly regarding the glass curvature, which is still being refined. The earliest version had a very pronounced curve; it was later reduced somewhat.

It’s standard practice for Apple to develop multiple competing prototypes of new devices, evaluating them for everything from usability and durability to ease of manufacturing.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

The curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. The actual visual effect could be quite stunning.

We yesterday saw an AI-generated render of what the design could look like. It’s expected to be the biggest redesign of the standard iPhone since the iPhone X.

With Thanksgiving almost here, it’s not too early for Broadway to start thinking about…March?

In case you’ve noticed a lot of big, starry announcements in recent weeks for shows that will open this spring – and not just spring proper like the Tony-heavy month of April, but the chillier weeks just after the December holidays but before the Easter thaw.

Why announce now? The better to entice potential ticket-buyers into surprising their beloveds with gift-wrapped tickets (or printed payment confirmations) to see Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd and Sarah Paulson this early March, or Steve Carell and John C. Reilly a week or two later. Merry Christmas, Happy Hanukkah and Happy Easter all rolled into one. Related Stories News 'Much Ado About Nothing' Broadway Review: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell & Jamie Lloyd Throw An Irresistible Party Of Shakespeare's Great Comedy News Josh Radnor & Beth Behrs To Join Broadway's 'Schmigadoon!'

Broadway’s upcoming winter season comes as a very star-packed fall is raking up strong weekly grosses. Last week, the critically-blessed Much Ado About Nothing starring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell grossed a whopping $2,352,287, while Crystal’s 860 broke the house record for a play at the Imperial Theatre with a big $1,720,253. Other Desert Cities, starring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery and Lily Rabe, grossed $2,570,589, a common enough occurrence for that show to place it week after week alongside such a $2M+ stalwart as Hamilton. Watch on Deadline

But Broadway won’t be resting on its pine-scented laurels for long: A week after the holidays, Manhattan Theatre Club’s Awake and Sing! revival starring West Wing‘s Richard Schiff, Jessica Hecht, Will Pullen, Danny Burstein and others opens January 7 (previews start December 15), and in short order the much anticipated Dolly: A True Original Musical (St. James Theatre) opens January 19 (previews start December 7) and Mix and Master, the Dominique Morisseau play starring Ruben Santiago-Hudson and Kara Young, begins previews January 5 at the Todd Haimes Theatre ahead of an opening night on January 27, 2027.

The March openings begin with Three Days of Rain, the Broadway revival of Richard Greenberg’s Pulitizer-finalist play with a big-name cast of François Arnaud, David Corenswet and Yvonne Strahovski. Performances begin Saturday, January 30, 2027, at the Longacre Theatre, with a March 1 opening night. It’s a 16-week engagement.

The Amish Project starring Jonathan Groff is a one-person play written Jessica Dickey, directed by Sarna Lapine, about an Amish community coming together in the wake of tragedy. Previews begin at the Broadhurst Theatre on February 10 ahead of an early March opening.

The starry month continues with Small Mouth Sounds, and, at least in terms of celebrity names, is the winter show to beat: Julia Roberts, Paul Rudd and Sarah Paulson lead the cast of Bess Wohl’s play that also includes Martin Freeman, Greta Lee and Isaac Powell. Joe Mantello directs, with Scott Rudin and Barry Diller producing. Previews begin February 10 at the Ethel Barrymore Theater, with an opening on March 11.

Next comes Dirty Dancing The Musical, starring Annalese Starzec and Blake Zelesnikar, both Broadway newcomers, but no matter: The star power of this one is the title itself, a name certain to stir nostalgia for fans of the Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze classic film romance. The new stage production based on the 1987 film will arrive on Broadway this winter for a limited seven-month engagement. Performances begin Friday, February 12, 2027, at Broadway’s Lena Horne Theatre with a “gala celebration” on Sunday, March 14.

Birthright, beginning previews February 23 at the Hudson ahead of a March 15 opening, carries the imprimatur of a very successful and acclaimed Off Broadway run last summer, along with the reputation of the playwright – Jonathan Spector – who scored a major Broadway success last year with the Tony-winning Eureka Day. Casting for the play hasn’t been announced, but the Off Broadway production starred such New York stage favorites as Molly Ranson, Nate Mann, Liz Larsen, Eli Gelb, Molly Bernard, Zoë Winters and Hale Appleman.

March’s final weeks will continue the celebrity appeal with The Odd Couple, starring Steve Carell, who will play the persnickety Felix Ungar, and John C. Reilly, as the slob Oscar Madison. Hamilton‘s Thomas Kail directs at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre, with performances for the 15-week engagement beginning March 3, 2027, and an opening on March 23.

And March goes out like a lion with Evita, director Jamie Lloyd’s revival of the Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber musical starring Rachel Zegler reprising her Olivier Award-winning performance as Eva Perón. Previews start February 27 at the Winter Garden – currently the home of Lloyd’s magnificent Much Ado – with an opening night of March 25.

Evita will be the final opening before the spring crunch of Tony-qualifying last minute arrivals goes full swing, and, yes, those shows will have plenty of stars as well – Jessica Chastain, Bryan Cranston, Laura Linney, Neil Patrick Harris and more. Those April openers include Gloria (April 5), Warriors (April 8), Purple Rain (April 12), All My Sons (April 13), The Sound of Music (April 15), Paddington The Musical (April 18), Montauk (April 19), Damn Yankees (April 20), Lost Lear (April 23) and Rhinoceros (April 25).

The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,249 (originally $1,499), the lowest price since Apple hiked prices this past summer. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3371. CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress To Pass AI Legislation To Protect Americans “Famous Or Not”

CAA chief Bryan Lourd is urging the full Congress to pass the No Fakes Act and deliver it to President Trump for signature, a move Lourd says would protect everyone, famous or not, from nonconsensual digital replicas of their voices and likenesses.

In a guest essay published in today’s New York Times, Lourd writes, “The Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature. That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era.”

The No Fakes Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and, Lourd contends, there “is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year.” He calles it “one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support.” Watch on Deadline

Hollywood, Lourd writes, “is not afraid of new technology.”

“The objection from actors, musicians and other creators is to a world in which anyone can use their face or voice without permission,” he writes. “In fact, many artists are already embracing A.I. on their own terms. Some of them are making deals with companies that are creating their A.I. likenesses, with their consent.”

Lourd poses the issue as not just for Hollywood. “A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements,” he writes. “Is all this legal? Right now, it’s an open question. But it shouldn’t be.”

“Hollywood doesn’t need America’s leaders to devise a new concept for new circumstances,” writes the chief executive and co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency. “We need them to extend and enforce the rules that already exist. The use of Americans’ faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short: You need to get permission, and you need to pay for the use.”

“This principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century,” he continues. “Whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person’s voice or likeness — famous or not.”

The No Fakes Act, Lourd says, “would apply a tried-and-true formula to the A.I. era: control, consent and compensation. It would set a uniform federal standard to replace outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind. Its supporters include all sides of the table: SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other performers; the Motion Picture Association, representing the studios; and tech companies including IBM, Google and OpenAI.”

Earlier this month, Lourd told Deadline’s Dominic Patten, that the issues around AI are “about the fundamental relationship between technological progress and creative rights, and who determines the value of creative work, who decides how that work is used, and whether creators will share in the opportunities AI creates.”

Read Deadline’s exclusive interview with Lourd here.

#3368. iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

Are you holding out for an iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2? Let us know in the comments.

#3367. Watermelon Expands Production Ambitions As It Seals Partnership With Qatar’s Film Committee

Watermelon Pictures and the Film Committee at Media City Qatar have announced a planned strategic partnership to develop and co-produce a slate of films telling stories from the Global South.

For Watermelon, the partnership marks a significant expansion into larger-scale, mainstream production.

Badie Ali and Hamza Ali launched their Chicago-based production and distribution company in 2024, with a mission to amplify Palestinian and other under-represented voices.

Until now, the company has focused mainly on distribution, with recent releases including The Voice of Hind Rajab, El Sett, Who Killed Alex Odeh? and American Doctor. Related Stories News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic

Its cofounders recently signaled to Deadline that they were working on a development slate, without going into detail. Watch on Deadline

The strategic partnership aims to combine Qatar’s infrastructure and resources as it seeks to grow the film and TV sector at home and regionally, and Watermelon’s access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and understanding of what resonates with audiences.

“When we founded Watermelon Pictures, our vision was to bring powerful stories to the big screen with an unwavering commitment to authenticity,” said Watermelon Pictures cofounder Badie Ali.

“Our partnership with the Film Committee at Media City Qatar is a major step toward realizing that promise, allowing us to tell these stories on a larger scale while remaining true to the people and places at their heart.”

Under the partnership, the parties would aim to shoot projects substantially in Qatar or structure them as Qatari co-productions.

They would also seek to involve Doha-based post-production companies and help eligible projects access the Qatar Screen Production Incentive (QSPI), creating opportunities for local crews, businesses, and creative talent while strengthening Qatar’s position as an international production hub.

“Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world. We also want the films we support to create work for crews and businesses in Qatar and give them experience they can carry into their next production,” said Hassan Al Thawadi, Chairman of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar.

The Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures will jointly identify projects for the initial slate. The proposed partnership is subject to definitive agreements and the required approvals, with projects to be considered individually. More details on specific projects are soon to be announced

“Too many compelling stories and perspectives, including those of Arab and Muslim communities, have historically been underrepresented in mainstream cinema. We see an enormous opportunity to change that. Our planned slate will span genres, challenge perceptions, and, above all, entertain. Our ambition isn’t simply to create space in the industry. It’s to compete at its highest level,” said Watermelon Pictures cofounder Hamza Ali.

The announcement of the planned partnership was made during the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, running from November 19 to 21 within the framework of the Doha Film Festival.

#3366. The Best Early Black Friday Smart Home Deals

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some substantial discounts on smart home devices, with savings ranging from $23 to $700 across security cameras, video doorbells, smart locks, home security systems, thermostats, and robot vacuums. Several products are more than 50% off, including indoor security cameras from Blink, Ring, and Arlo, while higher-end devices from Eufy and Roborock are seeing price cuts of hundreds of dollars.

You can also check out our other Black Friday coverage for more tech deals as the sale continues. For now, here are some of the best early Black Friday 2026 smart home deals worth checking out.

Named the best security camera of 2024 by PCMag, TP-Link’s Tapo MagCam C425 is now down to $54.99 from $89.99, making it an affordable option for keeping an eye on your driveway, backyard, or front entrance without having to run power cables. It records in 2K resolution and runs on a rechargeable battery, while support for microSD storage lets you save footage locally without paying for a cloud subscription.

Reolink’s 4K Solar Security Camera is down to $144.99 from $229.99, saving you $85. It connects over 4G LTE, so it can keep watch over a barn, vacation home, construction sites, or other areas where a regular wifi security camera won't work because there’s no home network to join. Its microSD support lets you save footage locally without a cloud subscription—you will, however, need an active cellular data plan to get the camera online.

Eufy’s SoloCam S340 is $119.99, down from $219.99, and it pairs a 3K wide-angle lens with a 2K telephoto lens, giving you a view of the whole yard and a closer look at faces or packages at the same time. The camera pans a full 360 degrees and tilts to follow people as they move, and the included solar panel keeps it charged in a sunny spot. Footage is stored on 8GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee—one of the reasons why the S340 earned an Editors’ Choice award in PCMag’s review.

Eufy’s Video Doorbell E340 is $99.99, down from $169.99, and it uses two cameras to cover your front door, with one recording visitors in 2K and the other pointing down at the doorstep to keep an eye on deliveries. It also has color night vision, a removable rechargeable battery, and 8GB of built-in storage for recording footage without a cloud subscription. You can read more about its performance in PCMag's review.

At $28, down from $79.99, the second-generation Arlo Wireless Video Doorbell 2K is one of the more affordable ways to keep an eye on your front door. Its 2K camera provides a detailed view of visitors, while the wide field of view helps capture packages left near your doorstep—making it easy to see why PCMag named it the best video doorbell of 2024.

The Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ is down to $34.99 from $79.99. It records in 2K resolution and offers a head-to-toe view, so you can see who's at the door as well as any packages left on your doorstep. And since it runs on batteries, installation is relatively simple, especially for renters or anyone who doesn't want to deal with doorbell wiring. For more on it, check out PCMag’s review.

The Eufy Security FamiLock E34 is down to $179.99 from $279.99, saving you $100 on a smart lock that uses palm vein recognition to unlock your door, which Eufy says takes just 0.6 seconds. It can store palm data for up to 50 people locally, making it convenient for households with multiple users, while PIN codes and app-based controls give you other ways to get inside. You also get built-in wifi and compatibility with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home, and Matter.

The Ultraloq Bolt Fingerprint smart lock is $139.99, down from $199.99, and it replaces your deadbolt with a lock you can open using a fingerprint, a keypad code, or the U Home app over built-in wifi. It can also unlock automatically as you walk up to the door, using your phone’s location. PCMag named it the best smart lock of 2024.

SimpliSafe’s DIY 8-piece Wireless Home Security System is down to $119.99 from $209.99, making it a relatively affordable starting point for securing multiple entry points around your home. The kit includes a base station, keypad, entry sensors, a motion sensor, and a panic button, so you can monitor doors, windows, and movement inside the house. The Arlo Home Security System is $142.49, down from $199.99, and this starter kit pairs a Keypad Sensor Hub with two All-in-One Sensors, each of which can be set to detect motion, open doors and windows, water leaks, and other events across eight functions. #3365. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

Proper balance becomes crucial in your senior years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As a certified personal trainer, I work with a wide range of clients who have lots of different fitness goals. But for my clients in their 60s and beyond, there’s usually one objective that drives their training: improving balance and stability.

I recently started working with a 60-year-old client who wanted to focus on just that. She noticed that she was a little more unsteady on her feet than she used to be, and had a few close calls with falling. After a thorough check-up with her doctor, we began our work together with the following routine.

These exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any new workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

These exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is important. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

You’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

Start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

You may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

During these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

#3362. ‘Artificial’ Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino On Whether AI Is Humanity’s Doomsday & Sam Altman’s Arsenal – Crew Call Podcast

Unlike Sony’s recent theatrical release of The Social Reckoning, which arguably didn’t resonate with the current tech era we’re living in, Neon is unwrapping Luca Guadagnino‘s Artificial about Open AI co-founders Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever and Elon Musk at a time when we fear the technology will end us.

Now whether that’s in regards to our existence or our financial livelihoods is another question.

Earlier this week, former OpenAI alum and Altman rival Dario Amodei’s Anthropic went public creating a $1.18 trillion company. However, shares fell from its $111 day-of-market price to $88.91 EOD Friday. Neon is shrewdly opening Artificial limited on Christmas Day (the perfect time to launch a sophisticated adult skewing awards contender), and in the run-up to that release, following premieres at New York Film Festival and BFI London Film Fest, along with current awards voter screenings, anticipation is boiling for the pic evident in its current 95% fresh Rotten Tomatoes critics rating. Related Stories News Timothée Chalamet Addresses Possibility Of A 'Call Me by Your Name' Sequel: "Never Say Never" News Sam Altman On 'Artificial' Movie About Him -- Not Among "Ten Weirdest Things In My Life" Right Now

As a filmmaker who knows something about love with the Zendaya starring tennis love triangle pic, Challengers, and Oscar winning gay romance, Call Me By Your Name, we spoke with Guadagnino on the latest Crew Call as to what pulled him into the OpenAI-verse. Watch on Deadline

Take a listen below. Essentially, it’s about about a bunch of young mad, narcissistic scientists acting like flawed Greek Gods in San Francisco:

Well before its theatrical release, Artificial generated a lot of controversy as its original studio, Amazon MGM Studios, backed away from the movie out of fear of OpenAI. That’s because Amazon has a $50 billion investment in the Altman non-profit.

However, unlike the Facebook camp back when Social Network was getting released in 2010, there’s been zero ill will coming from Altman or OpenAI about Guadaganino’s film. In fact, you could say they’re great sports.

In a sit-down with the Vanity Fair podcast, Altman says he “did not” coerce Amazon to drop Artificial. “I don’t know anyone else who did,” he added, “I didn’t speak to Jeff Bezos.”

In fact, Guadagnino brazenly shot the pic outside Altman’s house in San Francisco. The filmmaker tells us about that. For Altman, he was giddy about running into his onscreen doppelgänger, Andrew Garfield: “One morning, I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with the same backpack, walking so much, I felt like I was in a weird glitch or a simulation.”

Altman emphasized to Vanity Fair that Garfield “did walk like me.”

While Altman hasn’t seen Artificial, his reaction to the trailer is, “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy, so in that sense it doesn’t bother me. They’re trying to make a good movie and maybe it will be good. It won’t be good as an accurate depiction, except for the walk. I’m sure they’ll get other parts right at least accidentally.”

One of the jaw dropping moments shown in the Artificial trailer is Altman having a bunker in his wine country estate loaded with guns.

“That is an example of an inaccuracy,” Altman told Vanity Fair, “There’s no bunker with firearms on the wall.”

“I have a survivalist mindset,” Altman admitted, “but I don’t have a setup that is depicted in that trailer.”

Guadagnino tells Deadline, “I have validated the validating information that has been vetted: He does have guns.”

While the filmmaker experienced zero pushback from OpenAI and Altman during production on the Simon Rich script, he says “We were very careful that everything that was in the movie had to be approved legally, so that we were not bending facts and reality for our narrative purposes. But, because the truth in this case is more extraordinary than any fiction, that was okay. Because we had the drama, we had the juice.”

When it came to Amazon exiting Artificial, Guadagnino had a Zen mindset: “I was cool because I like disruptions, very much.”

“Their decision to give the movie to us to find another home was truly honorable, because they could have written off the movie and (said) ‘Bye-bye’.”

As far as Artificial being a hot potato that no studio wanted to handle, except NEON, Guadagnino asserts that “All the speculation about nobody wanting the movie; I like to think that there was the need (by the media) to fill blank pages with nothing.”

For off the bat, per Guadagnino, NEON was first, front and center in their passion to takeover the project after CAA screened it for them. Listen above for more details.

When it comes to the paranoia out there that AI is the catalyst for human extinction in ten years, the filmmaker tells Deadline, “I don’t have trust and I don’t have faith in humans.”

His suspicions about AI stem from growing up during the Cold War. “I remember very well in 1985 when Chernobyl happened,” he adds.

And there’s myriad reasons for concerns about AI, from a Chatbot being at the center of 16-year old Adam Raine’s suicide, to AI trespassing and impostering another company’s security space

We also talk with the Call Me By Your Name Best Picture Oscar nominee on why Andrew Garfield was the right guy to play Altman, and the Open AI Boss’ sincerity when it comes to creating guardrails for the technology.
