'Roman J. Israel' might be the best Denzel performance you've never seen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Verdict: If I were just judging Denzel Washington's performance, I'd probably give "Roman J. Israel, Esq." five out of five stars. Unfortunately, I have to grade the movie as a whole. Outside of Denzel's Oscar-nominated portrayal of the titular attorney, there's not much going for this legal thriller, which masquerades as a dramatic character study until its final act. It's still worth watching, but only just.

Where to watch: Stream "Roman J. Israel, Esq." for free on Pluto TV

Like most people, I have never seen "Roman J. Israel, Esq." I knew it would eventually come up in the Denzel Watchathon, but until recently, it was just a name on a list of movies to watch; presumably just an unremarkable piece of Denzel's impressive filmography.

But then something happened — I started getting fed clips from this movie on TikTok. Was the Chinese government spying on me, knowing that this movie was approaching in my 52-film journey through Denzel's career and trying to pique my interest? For legal reasons, I certainly can't claim that to be the case, but regardless of why these clips were suddenly in my algorithm, one thing was clear to me: Denzel is really good in this movie.

Turns out, I'm not the only person who got that impression, because the legendary actor was nominated for his eighth Oscar for his portrayal of the titular attorney.

However, that's essentially where the praise for this movie ends. Despite featuring future Oscar nominee Colin Farrell alongside Denzel, and a screenplay written by director Dan Gilroy (who, while not as accomplished as his brother Tony, has still written and directed some great movies), this movie fell flat critically and commercially. It is currently rated 55% fresh by critics on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences don't rate it much higher; just 57%. It brought in just $13 million on a $22 million budget, making it an undeniable flop despite featuring an award-worthy performance from Washington.

So with that knowledge in mind, I was ready to judge the movie for myself. Were the TikTok clips foreshadowing an excellent movie to come? Would I soon join the group of people underwhelmed by this film? Two hours later (plus some commercials), I had a definitive answer.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Pluto TV, one of the best free streaming services we've tested.

Malcolm has been with the Streaming team at Tom's Guide since 2023, reviewing dozens of movies each year so you don't have to watch the bad ones.

As already mentioned, "Roman J. Israel, Esq." stars Denzel Washington as the titular character. Roman is a partner at a small criminal defense firm in Los Angeles until, suddenly, his partner, William Jackson, has a heart attack and goes into a permanent coma. That leads Jackson's estate to bring in big-shot lawyer George Pierce (Colin Farrell), one of Jackson's former law students, to help wind down the firm's operations, as it turns out the partnership has been hemorrhaging money, unbeknownst to Roman.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

Roman isn't left looking for a job long, though. Pierce offers Roman a job at Pierce's firm, seeing Roman's clear talent as a legal mind. However, Roman quickly clashes with the culture at his new firm, and it's obvious why.

To be on the safe side, I'll describe Roman as a ... socially awkward character, but I think most people today would identify him as neurodivergent. He's a brilliant analyst of the law. His research is impeccable. But he has zero people skills and strong moral and ethical convictions that often lead him to butt heads with basically everyone he has a conversation with.

This forces Denzel to give a fairly uncharacteristic and complex performance. While Roman shares Denzel's proclivity for effortlessly spewing compelling dialogue, there's none of the gravitas that comes with Washington's more verbose, award-nominated performances. Roman has a well-educated, well-spoken tongue, but he doesn't have the smooth, silver tongue of someone like Alonzo in "Training Day," or even historical figures Malcolm X and Rubin "The Hurricane" Carter.

There's also a physical element to the performance. It's unclear whether he's wearing a relatively subtle fat suit, bulkier clothing, gained actual weight for the performance or some combination of the three, but Denzel as Roman is a noticeably larger figure than I typically associate with the actor. Not that he's ever diminutive on screen; he's as often an action star as he is a dramatic force of nature and typically he's in excellent shape. But the physique of Roman is one I'd associate more with Forest Whitaker than Denzel. In fact, I couldn't help but think about what the movie would be like with Whitaker, an incredible actor in his own right, as Roman instead of Washington.

For most of the movie, you'd be forgiven for fast-forwarding through every moment that isn't Denzel talking. The TikTok clips I mentioned in the introduction of this review? They're probably 90% of this movie that's worth watching. That is, until we get to the third act, when this legal thriller actually becomes ... well, thrilling.

Perhaps it's for the best that Denzel got the role, though, because it's essentially the movie's sole saving grace. Farrell isn't miscast, but he's woefully underutilized as Pierce, and it's not the most emotive performance, save for a few moments. Roman's love interest, Maya (Carmen Ejogo), has zero chemistry with Roman. It's awkward from beginning to end, and you almost want to fast-forward through their scenes together.

In fact, for most of the movie, you'd be forgiven for fast-forwarding through every moment that isn't Denzel talking. The TikTok clips I mentioned in the introduction of this review? They're probably 90% of this movie that's worth watching. That is, until we get to the third act, when this legal thriller actually becomes ... well, thrilling.

I don't want to spoil the twist that ultimately thrusts this legal thriller into its propulsive, paranoid conclusion. But I will say that Roman, normally so strong in his convictions, finally reaches a breaking point, and it's the first time in the movie that the character becomes interesting rather than merely a vehicle for impressive dialogue.

I realize that I've spent a few paragraphs talking about this film's lowlights, but despite its flaws, it's still a movie I recommend watching for anyone who loves a great Denzel performance. While the movie is far from the best he's ever been in, his performance is well-deserving of the Oscar nomination it earned. Now that I've seen it for myself, I'll freely admit that it's a quintessential part of his oeuvre and certainly merits inclusion on his highlight reel.

So while it's streaming for free, make sure to check out "Roman J. Israel, Esq." if you haven't already. And based on its meager box office returns, I'm willing to bet you haven't checked this movie off your own personal Denzel Watchathon.

#3358. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3357. iOS 27.3 adds Siri AI usage limits, here’s what counts toward your limit

Earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn

In a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

One question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The company shares just two examples of something advanced:

Suppose it gets it wrong like it does most of the time. I wonder if that still counts.

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”

It would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for users. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

What do you think of Siri AI’s parameters for advanced requests in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3355. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone company offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

Looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

This is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

My initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

The Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

Anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

So how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the users, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

However, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

So it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not important. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a big way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

That's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

If it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

#3348. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

#3347. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3343. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3342. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important issues and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

#3341. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3340. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3339. Instagram finally lets users edit Stories after publishing, but there’s a catch

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

Type: Memory foam and natural latexBest for: Combination sleepers and hot sleepersSizes: queen and king, standard and high loftTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1 yearPrice: $135 at Saatva

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is sold in a standard and high loft with a breathable cotton cover that’s removable and washable. Inside the cover is a mixture of memory foam and natural latex pieces that create a comfortable and huggable pillow. The shredded foam design worked well with the cotton cover to prevent any overheating at night.

I tested the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow in a standard loft and, though I sunk slightly into it, the pillow seemed to settle to the perfect height needed to sleep comfortably on my back and stomach.

While I could sleep on my side on the standard loft, I would suggest the high loft for side sleepers who need more support. This pillow gave me no reason to doubt its durability as it always returned to its shape when I got up in the morning.

A starting price of $135 does push the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow into the premium price tier, but it's not completely surprising for a luxury sleep brand like Saatva. However, you can sometimes catch a bundle deal that can save you up to $60 when you buy two.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is breathable and comfortable for all sleep types. Starting at $135, it’s a luxury buy, although for Black Friday you can save when you buy a pair of pillows. Buyers also receive a 45-night trial and one-year warranty when they order this pillow.

A standard queen size Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is $135, which puts it into a premium category. Saatva rarely, if ever, includes pillows in the monthly Saatva mattress sales, but it sometimes has cut-price deals on a pair of pillows during sales events such as the Black Friday mattress sales.

In fact, the current Saatva Black Friday mattress sales have a deal where you can save up to $60 when you buy two Cloud Memory Foam Pillows at Saatva.

If this pillow was filled solely with memory foam, I’d say it was overpriced. The natural latex added to the fill and a cotton cover make the price feel more reasonable, though I think a removable fill to make the height adjustable at home would make this pillow feel like better value.

Saatva offers a 45-night trial and a one-year warranty with the purchase of this pillow. Brands like Bearaby only offer 30-day trials, so an extra 15 days is nice, until you consider the generous trial offered with the Coop Adjustable Latex Pillow — 100 nights and 5 years warranty for some of its latex pillows.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow can be ordered in two sizes – queen and king – and two loft heights — standard and high. The standard loft is 4"-5" tall, while the high loft is 6"-7" in height.

This pillow has a breathable organic cotton knit cover (though it doesn’t have organic certifications) that’s removable and washable.

Despite the name of the pillow, the fill is comprised of both shredded gel-infused CertiPUR-US memory foam and natural latex foam. According to Saatva, the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is hypoallergenic.

I slept on the Helix Cooling Memory Foam Pillow for a week and performed a series of objective and subjective tests, following our pillow testing methodology.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a clear plastic bag within a cardboard box. It wasn’t vacuum sealed, meaning when I pulled it out of the plastic bag, it was ready to be slept on.

There weren’t any noticeable off-gassing smells when I pulled it from the packaging, but to be fair, I was really congested during the testing period because of hay fever.

However, when I slept on the pillow, there was an almond smell to it, which is a fairly common off-gassing scent for memory foam products.

The previous Saatva pillow I tested was too tall and didn’t have much give — which is why I breathed a sigh of relief the first time I laid my head on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

I tested a queen standard loft and discovered it to be the perfect size for someone like me who likes to sleep on her stomach, back, and side.

The shredded fill of this pillow spreads when weight is placed on it, but not enough that my head sunk down to the bed.

As I moved my head on the pillow, the pillow felt malleable and soft, hugging my head in a comforting way. I particularly like how this pillow feels when I’m lying on my back and stomach, as my head sinks enough to align my spine, lulling me to sleep quickly.

I can sleep on my side with the standard loft size. However, I think the high loft would be better if I was strictly a side sleeper.

When the pillow eventually breaks down, I can see myself sleeping on my side less and less with this pillow and reverting to my back or stomach. Those with broad shoulders should choose the high loft size from the get-go.

I placed a 15lb weight in the center of the pillow, and it sunk over an inch. That makes sense considering the foams inside are shredded. When I lifted the dumbbell, the pillow sprung back into shape immediately, which is a good sign of the its durability.

I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty when sleeping on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow, and that’s all thanks to Saatva’s temperature regulation. Memory foam is a far more heat-retaining material than natural latex, so to mitigate any overheating issues, Saatva utilized organic cotton for the cover — which is breathable — and shredded the memory foam and latex interior fill so air could weave its way through and keep my temperature neutral at night.

During the beginning of testing, I was sleeping without the air-conditioner and just a fan, so it was about 75 degrees in my house when I fell asleep at night and around 70 degrees when I woke up in the morning. The fact that heat did not build up during that time was very promising, and most likely what you can expect throughout the year.

A good rule of thumb: replace your pillows every two years and keep an eye on how quickly your pillow bounces back over time.

This can be done by folding your pillow in half. A slow bounce back means the fill has worn down. Until the pillow breaks down, maintenance will ensure it lasts longer.

After a week of testing, I haven’t noticed any sagging or break down of the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow. The shredded nature of the memory foam and latex fill means you may not be laying your head on the same bits of foam each night, which will probably result in a longer lifespan.

The cotton cover also appears durable, and if well maintained (i.e. washed) it should hold up for at least two years. If it does break down, you could easily replace the cover, but I don’t see that happening.

Thankfully, Saatva offers a one-year limited warranty on this pillow so if you notice anything out of the ordinary, take advantage of the warranty.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that I realized how important it is to take care of your pillow. They easily absorb sweat, night creams, and all manner of stuff from your head and face. Maintenance ensures they last longer.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is made of two parts — the cover and the fill. The cover can be removed and machine washed on cold on a delicate cycle, and either hung to dry or tumbled dry on low.

You can’t throw the memory foam and latex fill into the wash, but you can spot clean it if you need to.

Comfort is the most important thing to me when it comes to a pillow and the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow delivered.

The cloud-like and huggable surface is conducive to a good night’s sleep, especially since it’s supportive enough to keep your head and spine aligned no matter what position you sleep in. If you prefer to sleep on your side, I would order the high loft option, as it’ll offer more support for a longer period of time.

The cotton cover and the shredded natural latex and memory foam fill results in a breathable design, so you won’t sleep hot or sweat at night.

During the testing period, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow bounced back quickly, leading us to believe that it’ll last the full two years of a pillow's lifetime. Especially if you wash the cover consistently.

All in all, this supportive and huggable pillow will cradle your head and lead to a comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You overheat at night: This pillow is breathable, thanks to a cotton cover and an interior fill of shredded latex and memory foam.

✅ You're a combi sleeper: This pillow has the right amount of give and support for those who like to sleep on their stomach, back, and side. I suggest the high loft option for side sleepers.

✅ You like to try your pillow for a decent amount of time: Saatva lets buyers test a pillow for 45 days. If you don’t like it, Saatva will accept a return and give you a full refund.

❌ You prefer organic materials: This pillow does have some memory foam and while it’s CertiPUR-US certified, that doesn’t mean its free of toxins or VOCs, only that it’s low enough to be considered “safe.” Neither the natural latex, nor the organic cotton used in the fill and the cover are certified as organic despite claims by Saatva.

❌ You like to customize the size of your pillow: While you can order this pillow in high or low loft, unfortunately, Saatva didn’t design it so you could remove or add fill and thus adjust the height in your own home.

❌ You like a supportive, firm feel: Your head is going to sink into this soft and cloud-like pillow. For a more supportive and firm feel, try Saatva’s Down Alternative Pillow.

The Helix Talalay Latex pillow is a good alternative for those who don’t like their head sinking too far into their pillow as it’s made from a single piece of foam. Expect a bouncier feel. Made with Talalay latex and perforated with holes, this pillow will help you stay cool all night long. It comes in two loft options and you can get this pillow for as little as $111, which is more affordable than the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

As the name of this pillow indicates, the Coop Sleep Good Adjustable Latex Pillow is adjustable. It's made with a blend of natural Talalay latex and microfibers, and comes with an extra bag of fill so you can add more if necessary and create the loft and feel you prefer. Our reviewer reports that the pillow is breathable and prevents heat from trapping. A 100-night trial and a 5-year warranty is worth having, too.

If you want buttery soft comfort for a budget price, then I reccomend the viral Squishmallows SquishPillow, which is just $29.99 in a standard size. Currently our No 1 budget pick thanks to our glowing SquishPillow review (which praised its plush comfort and reliable support), the SquishPillow comes in a medium, firm or soft.
